explanations.explanation: That's the king's own read on it. He says, "Why is your face sad, though you are not ill? This could only be sadness of the heart." (Nehemiah 2:2) Artaxerxes, king of Persia, has seen Nehemiah pour wine for him plenty of times, and Nehemiah had never been sad in his presence. A king can tell when something's off, friend.

Good guess, but the king never says anything about work. He says it could only be "sadness of the heart." (Nehemiah 2:2) Artaxerxes, king of Persia, already knows Nehemiah isn't ill, so he goes straight for what's going on inside. Nehemiah's job is pouring wine, and I've seen cookie dough cause more stress than that.

Nothing in the passage says anything about a road, friend. The king says Nehemiah isn't ill, and then he says, "This could only be sadness of the heart." (Nehemiah 2:2) Artaxerxes, king of Persia, is looking at his heart, not his feet. Nobody had even mentioned a trip yet.

Not quite, baker. The text says, "I was overwhelmed with fear" right after the king speaks. (Nehemiah 2:2) Nehemiah was shaking on the inside, and the Bible doesn't hide it. I think anybody would be, with a king staring at them.

That's right. Nehemiah says, "I was overwhelmed with fear" when the king asks about his face. (Nehemiah 2:2) He wasn't calm and he wasn't cool. I've been there, friend, my knees knocking like a loose cookie sheet. He answers anyway, and that takes real courage.

explanations.answer: It lies in ruins and its gates are burned
explanations.explanation: Yes, and he says it plainly: "Why should I not be sad when the city where my fathers are buried lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?" (Nehemiah 2:3) Notice he doesn't say "Jerusalem." He calls it the city where his fathers are buried. I think that tells you how close to home it hits.

explanations.answer: Its people have all been carried away
explanations.explanation: Nehemiah never says that, friend. He says the city "lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire." (Nehemiah 2:3) His grief is about the city itself. Nothing in his answer is about where the people went.

explanations.answer: Its temple has been torn to the ground
explanations.explanation: The temple doesn't come up in his answer. He says the city "lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire." (Nehemiah 2:3) Gates and ruins are what he names. Stick to what the text says, baker, and you'll never get burned.

explanations.answer: Prays to the God of heaven
explanations.explanation: That's it. The king asks, "What is your request?" and the very next line says, "So I prayed to the God of heaven." (Nehemiah 2:4) The king is standing right there waiting, and Nehemiah still takes a moment to pray. I'd have blurted something out and then needed a nap.

explanations.answer: Asks the queen to speak for him
explanations.explanation: The queen is there, but she isn't asked to say anything for him. She shows up later as the one seated beside the king. (Nehemiah 2:6) What Nehemiah does before answering is this: "So I prayed to the God of heaven." (Nehemiah 2:4)

explanations.answer: Asks for a night to think
explanations.explanation: No night of thinking here, friend. The king asks his question, and right away Nehemiah "prayed to the God of heaven." (Nehemiah 2:4) Then he answers the king. It all happens in one conversation, and I think that's a pretty bold way to handle it.
That's the word. Nehemiah asks the king to send him to Judah "so that I may rebuild it." (Nehemiah 2:5) He isn't asking for a vacation, friend. He wants to put the city back together.

Close, but that's not the word he uses. Nehemiah asks the king to send him "so that I may rebuild it." (Nehemiah 2:5) The city is already in ruins, so there's nothing left to guard. He's going to build.
A visit would be a lot easier, wouldn't it? But Nehemiah asks the king to send him "so that I may rebuild it." (Nehemiah 2:5) He's not going to look around and come home. He's going there to work.

Yes, he does. The king, with the queen seated beside him, asks, "How long will your journey take, and when will you return?" (Nehemiah 2:6) A king who asks about your trip is already planning on letting you go. That's a good sign, baker.

Actually, he does ask. The king, with the queen seated beside him, says, "How long will your journey take, and when will you return?" (Nehemiah 2:6) After that, the text says it pleased the king to send Nehemiah. I'd call that a pretty good sign.

explanations.answer: So they'll grant him safe passage
explanations.explanation: Right on. Nehemiah asks for letters "so that they will grant me safe passage until I reach Judah." (Nehemiah 2:7) He's thinking ahead, friend. A letter from the king is like having the best pass in the whole kingdom.

Workers aren't part of that request. The letters are "so that they will grant me safe passage until I reach Judah." (Nehemiah 2:7) The governors are there to help him get through, not to supply a crew.

No money in this request, baker. Nehemiah asks for letters "so that they will grant me safe passage until I reach Judah." (Nehemiah 2:7) The letters are about getting there safely. The timber comes up in the next request.
That's the one. Nehemiah asks for "a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king's forest." (Nehemiah 2:8) Asaph looks after the trees, and Nehemiah needs wood. Makes sense to me, friend.

Close, but not quite. The text says, "a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king's forest." (Nehemiah 2:8) Nehemiah wants timber, and a forest is where the timber is. I've never baked a beam out of cookie dough, but I imagine it's no good.
Sheep can't build a wall, friend. Asaph is the "keeper of the king's forest," and he's the one who can give Nehemiah timber. (Nehemiah 2:8) Trees, not flocks.

explanations.answer: The gracious hand of his God was on him
explanations.explanation: That's what Nehemiah says himself: "because the gracious hand of my God was upon me, the king granted my requests." (Nehemiah 2:8) He doesn't pat himself on the back. He gives the credit to God, and I admire that. Nice lesson for all of us, friend.

explanations.answer: He had served the king for years
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give that as the reason. Nehemiah says, "because the gracious hand of my God was upon me, the king granted my requests." (Nehemiah 2:8) He points to God, not to his own time on the job.

explanations.answer: The king owed him a favor
explanations.explanation: No favors owed here, baker. Nehemiah says, "because the gracious hand of my God was upon me, the king granted my requests." (Nehemiah 2:8) He credits God, and the text doesn't say anything about a debt.
Not true, friend. The text says, "The king had also sent army officers and cavalry with me." (Nehemiah 2:9) Nehemiah got letters and an escort. He wasn't walking out there alone.

Yes, that's false. The text says, "The king had also sent army officers and cavalry with me." (Nehemiah 2:9) So he had soldiers riding along with him. That's a lot more company than I had in my old drawer, friend.

That's the word. Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite official "were deeply disturbed." (Nehemiah 2:10) Sanballat and Tobiah are brand new in the story, and they're already upset. They heard that someone was coming to help, and it bothered them.

Yes, that's the word. They were upset "that someone had come to seek the well-being of the Israelites." (Nehemiah 2:10) Nehemiah's whole trip is about helping people. And somebody still wasn't happy about it.

The text says they were "deeply disturbed," not amazed. (Nehemiah 2:10) Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite official did not hear this news and clap. Amazed would be a nicer reaction, friend, but that's not what the Bible says.

Ruin is in the story, but it's not the word in this blank. They were upset that someone "had come to seek the well-being of the Israelites." (Nehemiah 2:10) Nehemiah came to seek well-being, not ruin. The ruin is what he came to fix.
Worship isn't in this verse, baker. They were upset that someone "had come to seek the well-being of the Israelites." (Nehemiah 2:10) That well-being is what Nehemiah came to seek.
